title: Fieldwork Adventure: Foundations
welcome_lead: From measuring river depth to counting shoppers — fieldwork is geography in action. Let's start with basics.
meta_desc: GCSE Geography fieldwork basics — primary, secondary data, sampling, risk course.
final_note: You learned the difference between primary and secondary data and the main sampling methods.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Primary: you measure it. Velocity readings, pedestrian counts, environmental quality surveys.

Secondary: someone else already collected it. Census, OS maps, government data, newspaper reports.

Good investigations use BOTH.

You can't measure everything — so you sample.

Random: pick locations with random numbers — fair but can clump.

Systematic: every nth point (e.g. every 50m down a river) — easy and even.

Stratified: split population (e.g. high/middle/low income streets) — sample each group.

BEFORE going out you must assess risks:

Hazard: slippery river bank.
Risk: fall, hypothermia.
Control: wellies, work in pairs, stay close to bank.

You must also consider ethics: get permission, don't intimidate respondents, store data securely.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary data in geography fieldwork?
options: Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.
Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher (surveys, measurements, observations); secondary data already exists and is found in sources (census data, maps, published reports).
Primary data is more important and secondary data is less reliable.
Primary data is collected in primary schools and secondary data in secondary schools.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative data?
options: Quantitative data is always more scientific and reliable than qualitative.
Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.
Quantitative data is numerical and measurable (traffic counts, river width); qualitative data is descriptive and non-numerical (interview quotes, photo descriptions, field sketches).
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between random, stratified and systematic sampling?
options: All three sampling methods produce the same results.
Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.

Random: every member has equal chance of selection. Systematic: pick every nth item. Stratified: divide the population into groups and sample proportionally from each — ensures subgroup representation.
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.

sequence.def: Set the aim and a testable hypothesis before any fieldwork
Use sampling (random/systematic) to gather data in the field
Organise into tables, graphs and maps (e.g. choropleth)
Apply tests like Spearman's Rank to find relationships
Answer the hypothesis using the evidence gathered
Assess reliability, limitations and how to improve the study
